subject: Wondering about LKJ prior - is it really sensible? How to implement on constructed matrix?

messages.author: cf47bbe63da1f3ae
messages.subject: Wondering about LKJ prior - is it really sensible? How to implement on constructed matrix?
parts:
Have been trying to re-engineer the LKJ prior for use in a cholesky matrix constructed out of individual elements. Along the way I found that, in contrast to what I had been told / read here a few times before, setting an lkj_cholesky_corr(1) prior on a cholesky_factor_corr matrix *does* have a purpose - otherwise there are different priors for different correlations in the resulting correlation matrix. The contrast in the script below, between density plots for the fit with and fit without the lkj prior, on a 4x4 correlation matrix, shows this.

Further, I am wondering about a justification for the decreasing prior probability of high correlations as the number of dimensions increases. If I have started with a dataset of two variables that involves a single correlation, and then add another variable to my analysis, why should that decrease the probability of a high correlation between my first two variables? Does anyone have thoughts on this?  For those unfamiliar, the R script below compares the 4 vs 2 variable case.

Finally - can anyone help me implement the LKJ prior on a constructed matrix? It might get messy in here I'm not sure if I should create a 2nd post, but for the moment I put my current attempt below...

#### testing LKJ prior
require(rstan)

sm <- '
data{
int ndim;
int lkj;
}
parameters{
real dummy;
cholesky_factor_corr[ndim] cholcorrmat;
}
model{
dummy~normal(0,1);
if(lkj==1) cholcorrmat~lkj_corr_cholesky(1);
}
generated quantities{
matrix[ndim,ndim] corrmat_out;
corrmat_out = cholcorrmat * cholcorrmat\';
}
'
par(mfrow=c(3,1))
ndim=4
fit=stan(model_code=sm,data=list(ndim=ndim,lkj=0),iter=5000,chains=3)
summary(fit,fit@model_pars[grep('out',fit@model_pars)],)$summary
stan_dens(fit,pars=fit@model_pars[grep('out',fit@model_pars)])

fit=stan(fit=fit,data=list(ndim=ndim,lkj=1),iter=5000,chains=3)
summary(fit,fit@model_pars[grep('out',fit@model_pars)],)$summary
stan_dens(fit,pars=fit@model_pars[grep('out',fit@model_pars)])


ndim=2
fit=stan(fit=fit,data=list(ndim=ndim,lkj=1),iter=5000,chains=3)
summary(fit,fit@model_pars[grep('out',fit@model_pars)],)$summary
stan_dens(fit,pars=fit@model_pars[grep('out',fit@model_pars)])

parts:
On Monday, October 31, 2016 at 6:28:27 AM UTC-4, Charles Driver wrote:
Further, I am wondering about a justification for the decreasing prior probability of high correlations as the number of dimensions increases. If I have started with a dataset of two variables that involves a single correlation, and then add another variable to my analysis, why should that decrease the probability of a high correlation between my first two variables? Does anyone have thoughts on this?

The positive definiteness constraint means you cannot have independent prior beliefs about the correlations. In the 3x3 case, you can think of the density as

f(rho_{12} | rho_{13}, rho_{23}) * f(rho_{13}, rho_{23})

Why should f(rho_{12} | rho_{13}, rho_{23}} in the 3x3 case be the same as f(rho_{12}) in the 2x2 case? Of course, in the 3x3 case, you can also think of the density as

f(rho_{12}) * f(rho_{13}, rho_{23} | rho_{12})

but then you have to have weird beliefs about rho_{13} and rho_{23} given rho_{12} if your beliefs about rho_{12} are the same as in the 2x2 case. Basically, rho_{13} and rho_{23} have to be more concentrated near zero than rho_{12} is to satisfy the positive definiteness constraint.

For K > 6, increasing K decreases the hypervolume of correlation matrices satisfying the positive definiteness constraint and the ones that do tend to be close to the identity matrix. To construct one, you are better off using the onion method, which yields the same distribution of correlation matrices. Search for onion.stan in Google Groups.

Ben

rscript to generate and plot distributions of random correlation matrices built up from elements (with a few tweaks edited in hours after initial post):

sm2 <- '
functions{

row_vector vecpower(row_vector vec, real power){
row_vector[num_elements(vec)] out;
for(i in 1:num_elements(vec)){
out[i] = vec[i]^power;
}
return out;
}

out[i]=sqrt(vec[i]);
}
return out;
}

matrix cholcor_lp(matrix mat, int chol, real eta){ //converts from lower partial cor matrix to cholesky cor
  int ndim;
  matrix[rows(mat),cols(mat)] mcholcor;
  real betad;
 
  ndim = cols(mat);
  mcholcor=diag_matrix(rep_vector(0,ndim));
  betad = eta + (ndim-1)/2;
  mcholcor[1,1]=1;

 
  if(ndim > 1){
    betad = eta + (ndim-1)/2;
    for(coli in 1:ndim){
      betad = betad - .5;
      for(rowi in coli:ndim){
        if(rowi > coli) mat[rowi,coli]/2+.5 ~ beta(betad,betad);
        if(coli==1 && rowi > 1) mcholcor[rowi,coli] =  mat[rowi,coli];
        if(coli > 1){
          if(rowi == coli) mcholcor[rowi,coli] = prod(vecsqrt(1-vecpower(mat[rowi,1:(coli-1)],2)));
          if(rowi > coli) mcholcor[rowi,coli] = mat[rowi,coli] * prod(vecsqrt(1-vecpower(mat[rowi,1:(coli-1)],2)));
        }
      }
    }
  }
  return mcholcor;
}

}
